articles.title: How to read a website

body.support:
Most websites have the same parts.

- **URL**: the address. *.gov.au* means a government site.
- **Navigation**: the menu at the top.
- **Homepage**: the main page.
- **About**: who runs it.
- **Contact**: how to reach them. A real phone number and address are good signs.
- **Footer**: the bottom of the page.

**Why was it made?** To inform? To sell? To trick you? Look at the biggest button. It shows what they want you to do.

**Is it real?** Check:

- Does the URL match the name?
- Are there real contact details?
- What do other sites say? Search the name with *scam*.

**Compare** two sites. You'll see what's missing.
body.core:
Websites look different, but most are built from the same parts. Know the parts, and you can find what you need, and spot what doesn't add up.

**The parts of a website**

- **URL**: the address. The **domain** (like *asic.gov.au*) tells you who owns it. *.gov.au* means an Australian government site. *.edu.au* is an education provider. *.com.au* is a business, but anyone can buy one.
- **Header and navigation**: the logo and menu at the top, which help you move around.
- **Homepage**: the main page. It shows what the site is mostly about.
- **About page**: who runs it. Real organisations give details: names, history, an address.
- **Contact page**: how to reach them. A real phone number and address are good signs. Only a form or a chat app is a warning sign.
- **Footer**: the bottom of the page, often with the business name, ABN, privacy policy and terms.

**Purpose and audience.** Every site is built for a reason: to **inform** (a government site), to **sell** (a shop), to **persuade** (a campaign), to **entertain**, or sometimes to **trick** you. Look at who it's talking to and what it wants you to do. The biggest button on the page usually tells you.

**Is it reliable?** Check:

- Does the URL match the organisation? Scam sites often copy real names with small changes.
- Are there real contact details?
- Is the information current and accurate?
- What do **other** sources say? Search the name with *reviews* or *scam*. For investments, check ASIC's **Investor Alert List**.
- A padlock means the connection is **secure**, not that the site is honest.

**Compare.** Looking at two sites side by side (two TAFE providers, two phone plans) shows you what's missing from one, and what's too good to be true.
body.extend:
Websites are structured digital texts. Their standard features help you find your way around. They also give you evidence for judging whether to trust the site.

**The features**

- **URL and domain:** the domain shows who owns the site. Only Australian government bodies can use *.gov.au*, and *.edu.au* is for education providers. Anyone can easily register a *.com.au* or *.com*.
- **Header and navigation:** organise the content and show what the site thinks matters most.
- **Homepage:** sets out the site's main purpose and audience.
- **About and Contact pages:** real organisations give details you can check. If these are missing, or you can only make contact through a form or a chat app, be careful.
- **Footer:** usually has the legal name, ABN, privacy policy and terms.

**Purpose and audience.** Sites may inform, sell, persuade, entertain or deceive. The **call to action** (the biggest button or link) usually shows the purpose. The language, images and design show who it's for.

**Judging reliability**

- Does the domain match the organisation, or copy it with small changes?
- Can you check the contact details?
- Is the information current, accurate and sourced?
- Do **independent** sources back it up? For investments, ASIC's **Investor Alert List** flags suspicious businesses.
- A padlock means the connection is **secure** (encrypted). It doesn't mean the owner is honest.

**Comparing** similar sites side by side shows you what's normal, what's missing, and which claims don't hold up.

caseStudies.title: Twelve thousand fake websites

body.support:
**ASIC** is a government group. It protects people from money scams.

In **2025**, it took down **11,964** scam websites. That's about **32 every day**!

Scammers now use **AI** to make fake websites fast. They look real. They have logos and happy photos.

So check:

- the URL
- the contact details
- what other sites say.

Too good to be true? It probably is.
body.core:
**ASIC** is the government agency that looks after Australia's financial rules. One of its jobs is protecting people from **investment scams**: fake websites that promise big returns, then steal your money.

In **2023**, ASIC started a service to get scam websites taken down. In **2025** alone, it removed **11,964** phishing and investment scam websites. That's about **32 websites every day**, and **90%** more than the year before.

ASIC warned that scammers are now using **AI** to build fake websites faster, and to make them look more convincing. Many copy the look of real businesses. Some use fake photos of famous Australians to pretend they're endorsed.

Why does this matter for you? Because scam websites don't look like scams. They have logos, menus, team photos and reviews, just like real ones. The only way to tell is to read them like a detective: check the URL, the contact details and the claims, and check what **other** sources say.

If an offer seems too good to be true, it almost certainly is.
body.extend:
**ASIC** is Australia's financial regulator. In **2023**, it started a service to take down investment scam and phishing websites.

From **1 January to 31 December 2025**, ASIC had **11,964** of these websites removed. That's about **32 a day**, and **90%** more than the year before.

ASIC said scammers are using **AI** to build fake sites faster and make them more convincing. Many copy real businesses. Some use fake endorsements from famous people.

This matters for how you read websites. Scam sites copy the features of real ones: logos, menus, About pages and reviews. You can't tell them apart from how they look. You have to judge them on evidence that's harder to fake. Does the domain match? Can you check the contact details? Are the claims accurate? And do independent sources, like ASIC's Investor Alert List, back them up?

**Website:** headspace.org.au

**Structure:** The top menu has four main sections. There is a search bar, and a “Find a centre” button on every page.

**Purpose:** To inform young people about mental health, and to connect them with help.

**Audience:** People aged 12 to 25. The language is plain and the photos show young people.

**Do I trust it? Yes.** The “About” page shows it is funded by the Australian Government. It does not sell anything, and it has clear contact details.

**Compared with:** a wellness blog that sells supplements and names no authors.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** URL (address and owner), navigation (move around), homepage (main purpose), About (who runs it), Contact (how to reach them), footer (official details). .edu.au is an education provider. A padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the owner is honest.

**Website:** 1 URL (.edu.au); 2 navigation (main sections); 3 image and headline (audience); 4 call to action (purpose); 5 real contact details; 6 footer (official details).

**Sort:** guaranteed 30% — warning; address, phone and ABN — good; asic-gov-invest.com — warning; WhatsApp only — warning; celebrity photo — warning; on ASIC's register — good.

**Case study:** they copy the features of real sites (logos, menus, photos, reviews). Easy to fake: logos, photos, testimonials, padlocks. Harder: a matching domain, a verifiable address and phone, independent reviews, appearing on official registers. Check: search the name with *scam*, check ASIC's Investor Alert List and professional registers, look for real contact details.

realityCheck: **Never click links on scam sites in class.** Use screenshots from Scamwatch or Moneysmart.
**Students trust polish.** The case study works best when you show how professional scam sites look.
**Pick relevant pairs.** TAFE providers, job boards and phone plans are things VM students actually compare.
**Some families have been scammed.** Keep it practical and non-judgemental.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It links to Lock It Down and to research skills from Research Ready.
